executive_assessment.text: Ethiopia faces robust warming and increasing heat risk, alongside recurrent drought/flood exposure and much greater uncertainty over future mean rainfall than over temperature. Supporting evidence: ETH-E-001-005; pathways ETH-P-001-003.

The strongest Climate-FCV mechanisms are mediated by food security, pastoral mobility/resource access, household assets and institutional/service capacity; evidence does not justify a general claim that climate change causes Ethiopian conflict. Supporting evidence: ETH-E-010-012, ETH-E-020-021; pathways ETH-P-001, ETH-P-002, ETH-P-004-007. (World Bank2)

Ethiopia has substantial policy, early-warning and programme capacity, but large implementation, monitoring, subnational-finance and conflict-sensitivity gaps constrain demonstrated resilience outcomes. Supporting evidence: ETH-E-013-019; ETH-P-005 and ETH-P-008.

coverage.value: Warming robust; drought/flood recurrent; future heat and heavy-rain intensity increase.
Rural climate-dependent livelihoods, pastoral lowlands and informal urban settlements are materially exposed.
coverage.gap_note: Limited recent nationally comparable exposure disaggregation.

coverage.value: Food poverty, rain-fed livelihoods, insecure tenure and displacement increase sensitivity.
coverage.gap_note: Some underlying statistics are older or operational.

coverage.value: Early warning, mobility, safety nets and household coping documented.
Large national policy architecture plus recent lowland investments.
Strong formal architecture but major regional/woreda finance, mandate and M&E gaps.
coverage.gap_note: Cross-region comparative institutional evidence remains thin.

coverage.value: Independent evaluation finds genuine SLM gains but important distributional/implementation limitations.
Food insecurity and mobility pathways supported, but causal attribution remains limited/local.
Insurance, customary dispute management and conflict-sensitive targeting have plausible/local support.

coverage.gap_note: Highland ecosystem projections less developed than heat/flood evidence.
Health and education service causal evidence is comparatively thin.
Community/customary evidence concentrated in pastoral settings.
Current 2024-26 programmes generally lack independent impact evaluation.

geographic_notes.text: National climate evidence is strongest for temperature, broad hazard exposure, policy architecture and institutional systems. The evidence repeatedly shows why national averages should not be transferred mechanically to subnational settings: eastern/northern lowlands face especially high heat exposure; pastoral lowlands have distinct mobility, tenure and water-access institutions; and urban informality creates different flood, heat and service vulnerabilities. (World Bank2)

*Somali Region evidence is unusually rich for the pastoral climate-security pathway, but SIPRI’s qualitative findings must remain explicitly subnational. Similarly, IEG’s land-restoration findings concern selected watersheds in Amhara, Oromia and Tigray rather than Ethiopia as a whole. (SIPRI7)

Contemporary conflict and humanitarian evidence is temporally sensitive. Current WFP material identifies insecurity in Amhara and broader displacement/insecurity as current operational constraints, but conditions and territorial access can change rapidly; the packet therefore does not extrapolate these claims to all regions. (World Food Programme8)

Important underrepresented areas/populations include smaller pastoral and agropastoral settings outside Somali Region, conflict-affected communities with poor research access, displaced people disaggregated by duration/status, people with disabilities, women’s differential control over adaptation resources, and city-level comparisons outside broad national urban evidence.

sector_notes.text: *Relatively well covered: agriculture, pastoral livelihoods, rangelands, food security, land management, disaster-risk management, social protection and humanitarian delivery.
*Moderately covered: water access, urban land/service vulnerability, irrigation, climate information and institutional coordination. (World Bank2)

*Thin for Climate-FCV purposes: hydropower, health-system resilience, education continuity, transport disruption, industrial/urban heat exposure and transboundary water politics. No transboundary dam or water-political dispute is coded here as a climate impact because the verified evidence does not establish that characterization.

known_gaps.text: Climate projections: Temperature projections are robust relative to precipitation, but subregional precipitation, drought-duration and highland ecosystem projections have significant model/spatial uncertainty. (World Bank2)

Causal Climate-FCV evidence: The available national evidence is mainly observational association and expert synthesis; the most specific mobility-conflict evidence is local to Somali Region. (World Food Programme1)

FCV -> adaptation: Conflict clearly constrains household welfare and humanitarian operations, but few studies quantify how conflict changes adaptation project performance, maintenance, climate-information use or resilience outcomes. (World Bank2)
Geographic coverage: Accessible evidence is uneven across conflict-affected locations and pastoral areas; rigorous local evidence should not be generalized to regions not studied.

Differentiated vulnerability: Gender is prominent in policy documents, yet the 2025 stocktake identifies implementation/tracking shortcomings; robust outcome data disaggregated by gender and other intersecting vulnerabilities remain limited.
Evaluation: Recent lowland resilience, irrigation, humanitarian and data-system investments mainly have output or programme-theory evidence, not independent impact estimates. (World Food Programme12)

Unintended effects: IEG and SIPRI identify credible adaptation/programme trade-offs - grazing restrictions and targeting-related tensions - but systematic monitoring of such effects is uncommon. (Independent Evaluation Group13)
Monitoring: Nearly two-thirds of the NDC adaptation indicators examined in the 2025 stocktake were untracked, materially limiting assessment of national adaptation progress.
Humanitarian data: Current WFP reporting is valuable for operational conditions but is not a substitute for representative household, displacement or service-delivery surveys. (World Food Programme8)

Access limitations: The official NAP is publicly listed, but the Ministry-hosted PDF timed out in this browsing environment; no page-specific NAP claim was therefore retained solely from that file. (Climate Change Portal4)

*None are wholly unsupported, but direct-climate-fcv and resilience-peace-capacity are only partially covered because much of the evidence is correlational, qualitative and geographically restricted. FCV-to-adaptation outcome evidence is also substantially thinner than evidence showing general FCV constraints on welfare and humanitarian delivery.
